item.title: Fluctuations in Environmental Resource Availability Alter the Oscillatory Tragedy of the Commons
item.description: arXiv:2611.06156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Environmental noise in real-world complex systems--including fluctuations in temperature, humidity, and related environmental conditions--inevitably modulates individual metabolic capacity and, consequently, the efficiency of public-resource utilization. Yet conventional evolutionary game models incorporating environmental feedback treat resource dynamics deterministically. Here, we incorporate stochastic fluctuations into a noise-corrected replicator-dynamics framework. Theoretical analysis and stochastic birth-death simulations yield a counterintuitive result: moderate environmental noise stabilizes, rather than destabilizes, the interior fixed point across diverse payoff landscapes, while suppressing or eliminating catastrophic oscillations. These findings reframe environmental variability not merely as a perturbation but as a mechanism that fosters strategy coexistence and sustainable resource use in complex social and ecological systems.
item.dc:creator: Yi-Duo Chen, Zhi-Xi Wu, Jian-Yue Guan

item.title: Phase Locking in Oscillator Networks with Uncertain and State-Dependent Couplings
item.description: arXiv:2611.06466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phase locking in oscillator networks depends critically on the interaction strengths between coupled units. In many applications, however, these couplings are uncertain, state dependent, or time varying. We derive rigorous conditions for phase locking in Kuramoto-type networks when each coupling strength is known only within prescribed bounds. Building on a convex formulation of the nonlinear fixed-point equations, we obtain edge-wise error bounds for arbitrary feasible approximations that hold uniformly over all admissible couplings. These bounds yield sufficient conditions for the existence of phase-locked states with prescribed phase-difference limits. We illustrate the framework for AC power grids with uncertain voltage magnitudes and adaptive oscillator networks with state-dependent couplings. For the latter, the bounds can be further tightened by exploiting the state dependence of the couplings.
item.dc:creator: Iva Ba\v{c}i\'c, Philipp C. B\"ottcher, Marc Hunkem\"oller, Carsten Hartmann, David Gross, Andrea Benigni, Dirk Witthaut

item.title: Emergent Incompressibility in Polariton Condensates for Scalable XY Spin Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.05782v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Driven-dissipative polariton networks offer a powerful analog platform for simulating continuous-spin Hamiltonians. However, their practical scalability is fundamentally limited by amplitude-phase coupling and metastable trapping in highly frustrated energy landscapes. Here, we present an \textit{in situ} dual-enhancement mechanism to address these bottlenecks without requiring external site-specific fine-tuning. First, a renormalization-group analysis based on density rescaling shows that higher-order nonlinear loss drives the condensates toward an incompressible regime, intrinsically suppressing amplitude fluctuations and enforcing phase-only dynamics. For macroscopic XY networks (up to 10,000 spins), this phase-amplitude decoupling yields a more than 50-fold reduction in energy, while simultaneously shrinking the standard deviation by a factor of six. More generally, it restores the extensive scaling of the optimized XY energy with system size. Second, to navigate the rugged, nonconvex energy landscape, we introduce weak Hermitian pulses. When implemented through a multistage protocol, these pulses enable repeated escapes from local minima and drive the system to deeper energy minima. Benchmarking shows an increasing advantage with system size, with the polariton simulator outperforming the classical Monte Carlo-SQP baseline in every sampled macroscopic realization. Our work provides a physical framework for scalable polariton analog computing.
item.dc:creator: Chengyong Yu, Youya Xu, Xuan Ye, Yan Zhou, Sanjib Ghosh

item.title: Inferring Coupled Stuart-Landau Equations from Waveforms
item.description: arXiv:2602.13031v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a physics-informed, data-driven framework for inferring phase-amplitude equations of coupled limit-cycle oscillators from waveform measurements. Guided by normal-form theory near a supercritical Hopf bifurcation, we infer a near-identity transformation from two observables of an isolated oscillator to a complex-amplitude coordinate, together with the intrinsic Stuart-Landau dynamics. Applying this transformation to coupled oscillators then enables estimation of the leading-order linear coupling terms. Using coupled van der Pol oscillators as an analytical benchmark, we demonstrate accurate inference under system noise and quantify the validity range with respect to the Hopf bifurcation parameter and coupling strength. Moreover, a model inferred from one informative trajectory at each coupling condition reproduces synchronized states and their basin structure for initial conditions not used in the inference. Applied to a high-dimensional hydrodynamic system, the inferred model captures bistability between in-phase and anti-phase synchronization and identifies the loss of anti-phase synchrony as a Neimark-Sacker bifurcation. Our framework provides a practical route from experimentally accessible waveforms to an interpretable normal-form model for stability and bifurcation analysis.
item.dc:creator: Yuki Araya, Hiroaki Ito, Hiroshi Kori, Hiroyuki Kitahata

item.title: Clustering without geometry in sparse networks with independent edges
item.description: arXiv:2603.13159v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The coexistence of sparsity and clustering (non-vanishing average fraction of triangles per node) is one of the few structural features that, irrespective of finer details, are ubiquitously observed across large real-world networks. This fact calls for generic models producing sparse clustered graphs. Earlier results suggested that sparse random graphs with independent edges fail to reproduce clustering, unless edge probabilities are assumed to depend on underlying metric distances that, thanks to the triangle inequality, naturally favour triadic closure. This observation has opened a debate on whether clustering implies (latent) geometry in real-world networks. Alternatively, recent models of higher-order networks can replicate clustering by abandoning edge independence. In this paper, we mathematically prove, and numerically confirm, that a sparse random graph with independent edges, recently identified in the context of network renormalization as an invariant model under node aggregation, produces finite clustering without any geometric or higher-order constraint. The underlying mechanism is an infinite-mean node fitness, which also implies a power-law degree distribution. Further, as a novel phenomenon that we characterize rigorously, we observe the breakdown of self-averaging of various network properties. Therefore, as an alternative to geometry or higher-order dependencies, node aggregation invariance emerges as a basic route to realistic network properties.
item.dc:creator: Alessio Catanzaro, Remco van der Hofstad, Diego Garlaschelli
